stem: A new potential blood test for diagnosing Alzheimer disease is evaluated in Populations A and B. The negative predictive value is estimated at 98% in Population A and at 85% in Population B. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?

options.A: The accuracy of the test is greater in Population A than in Population B
options.B: The prevalence of Alzheimer disease is greater in Population A than in Population B
options.C: The proportion of patients without Alzheimer disease is greater in population A than in population B
options.D: The sensitivity of the test is lower in Population A than in Population B
options.E: The specificity of the test is greater in Population A than in Population B

explanations.A: The accuracy of a diagnostic test is the probability that an individual is correctly classified by the test: accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN). Because no information is given on these specific values, no conclusions regarding accuracy can be made.
explanations.B: In this case, the test has a higher NPV (98%) in Population A than in Population B (NPV = 85%). This implies that Population A has a lower disease prevalence than Population B.
explanations.D: Sensitivity and specificity are intrinsic test parameters that are not affected by disease prevalence. The same test was used in Populations A and B, so there is no change in sensitivity and specificity.
explanations.E: Sensitivity and specificity are intrinsic test parameters that are not affected by disease prevalence. The same test was used in Populations A and B, so there is no change in sensitivity and specificity.

generalExplanation:
The negative predictive value (NPV), the probability that an individual truly does not have a disease given a negative test result, is equal to the number of individuals without disease and who test negative (ie, true negatives [TN]) divided by all those with a negative test result (ie, TN + false negative [FN]):
NPV = TN / (TN + FN)

Similarly, the positive predictive value (PPV), the probability that an individual truly has the disease (ie, true positive [TP]) given a positive test result (including TP or false positive [FP] results), is given by:
PPV = TP / (TP + FP)

Predictive values depend on disease prevalence in a population of interest. Specifically, disease prevalence affects NPV by changing TN and FN.
• Populations with exceptionally low disease prevalence (eg, prevalence close to 0%) have almost all TN (ie, more TN) with almost no TP (ie, fewer TP), and most positive tests would be FP (ie, more FP) with almost no FN (ie, fewer FN). This explains why NPV increases (more TN, fewer FN) and PPV decreases (fewer TP, more FP) with decreasing prevalence.
• Populations with exceptionally high disease prevalence (eg, prevalence close to 100%) have almost all TP (ie, more TP) with almost no TN (ie, fewer TN), and most negative tests would be FN (ie, more FN) with almost no FP (ie, fewer FP). This explains why NPV decreases (fewer TN, more FN) and PPV increases (more TP, fewer FP) with increasing prevalence.

In this case, the test has a higher NPV (98%) in Population A than in Population B (NPV = 85%). This implies that Population A has a lower disease prevalence than Population B (Choice B). Therefore, the proportion of patients without Alzheimer disease is greater in population A than in population B.
educationalObjective: Predictive values depend on disease prevalence. As disease prevalence increases, the positive predictive value increases and the negative predictive value decreases.

stem: A study was conducted to establish the average level of total serum cholesterol in a group of patients with acute coronary syndrome. The study results were reported separately for males and females. The mean total cholesterol level was 230 mg/dL for males and 220 mg/dL for females. Which of the following is the best statistical method to compare the average cholesterol level for males and females?

options.A: Two-sample t test
options.B: Two-sample z test
options.C: Analysis of variance (ANOVA)
options.D: Chi-square test
options.E: Meta-analysis

explanations.B: The two-sample z test can also be used to compare two means, but population (not sample) variances are employed in the calculations. Because population variances are not usually known, the test has limited applicability.
explanations.C: The ANOVA (i.e., analysis of variance) is used to compare three or more means.
explanations.D: The chi-square test is appropriate for categorical data and proportions.
explanations.E: Meta-analysis is an epidemiologic method of pooling the data from several studies to do an analysis having a relatively big statistical power.

generalExplanation: The two-sample t test is commonly employed to compare two means. Several statistical approaches can be used, but the basic requirements needed to perform this test are the two mean values, the sample variances, and the sample size. The t statistic is then obtained to calculate the p value. If the 'p' value is less than 0.05, the null hypothesis (that there is no difference between two groups) is rejected, and the two means are assumed to be statistically different. If the 'p' value is large, the null hypothesis is retained.
educationalObjective: The two-sample t test is a statistical method that is commonly employed to compare the means of two groups of subjects.

stem: A group of gynecologists conducted a study to determine if there is an association between hysterectomy and hyperlipidemia. They collected data from insurance claims of 5,900 women with a history of hysterectomy between 2000 and 2013, and of 18,500 women without any surgeries who were frequency-matched by birth year and surgery year to the women with hysterectomy. By the end of a 5-year period, both groups of women were ascertained for hyperlipidemia. The results of the study showed that there is a statistically significant association between hysterectomy and hyperlipidemia. The study concluded that women who undergo hysterectomy should routinely monitor their metabolic status. Which of the following statements is true about this study design?

options.A: It can consider only a single risk factor
options.B: It can study only a single outcome
options.C: It is not able to provide a true measure of risk
options.D: It may be affected by exposure misclassification
options.E: It may be affected by recall bias

explanations.B: Once participants are categorized based on exposure status, the incidence of ≥1 outcomes of interest (eg, hyperlipidemia) within a specific period (ie, 5 years) is determined and compared between groups to estimate the association between risk factor and outcome.
explanations.C: Because of these features, cohort studies can provide a true measure of risk of disease.
explanations.D: Exposure misclassification occurs when the risk factor under investigation is not identified correctly. In this study, it is very unlikely that the exposure (hysterectomy) was misclassified.
explanations.E: Inaccurate recollection of past events, known as recall bias, is a potential problem for case-control studies (not cohort studies), particularly when questionnaires are used to ask participants about distant past exposure.

generalExplanation:
This study has a cohort design in which potential participants are initially identified as exposed or nonexposed according to their exposure status to a risk factor (eg, hysterectomy). Because participants are categorized based on their status to a particular risk factor, a cohort study is able to consider only a single risk factor (ie, hysterectomy) per study.

Once participants are categorized based on exposure status, the incidence of ≥1 outcomes of interest (eg, hyperlipidemia) within a specific period (ie, 5 years) is determined and compared between groups to estimate the association between risk factor and outcome (Choice B). Because of these features, cohort studies can provide a true measure of risk of disease (Choice C).
educationalObjective: A cohort study begins by identifying individuals as exposed or nonexposed to 1 risk factor and ends by comparing the incidence of ≥1 outcomes (ie, disease) between the 2 groups.

stem: A prospective cohort study was conducted to assess the relationship between caffeine consumption and the risk of colon cancer in middle-aged women. The study showed that caffeine consumption decreases the risk of colon cancer with a relative risk of 0.83 and p value of 0.04. The fact that the study was conducted specifically in middle-aged women raises most concerns regarding which of the following issues?

options.A: Bias
options.B: Generalizability
options.C: Internal validity
options.D: Reliability
options.E: Reproducibility

explanations.A: In this scenario, there is no description of how the study was designed, conducted, and analyzed, so it is not possible to determine whether the internal validity was violated (ie, if bias is present).
explanations.C: Within this cohort (middle-aged women), the study could be valid. This property is called internal validity, or validity as generally taught.
explanations.D: Reliability or reproducibility is the measure of random error.
explanations.E: Reliability or reproducibility is the measure of random error.

generalExplanation: The generalizability, or external validity, of a study is defined as the applicability of the obtained results beyond the cohort that was studied. External validity answers the question, "How generalizable are the results of a study to other populations?" In this study, the external validity seems to be quite limited due to the restriction of the study population to middle-aged women. In other words, because the cohort is restricted to middle-aged women, the results of the study are applicable only to middle-aged women. This is an important concept when applying the results of observational studies and clinical trials to everyday practice if the original inclusion and exclusion criteria are not reviewed carefully. The other answer options are relevant for internal validity answering the following question: "Are the results obtained in this specific cohort valid?"
educationalObjective: Generalizability or external validity pertains to the applicability of study results to other populations (eg, the results of a study in middle-aged women would not be expected to be applicable to elderly men).

stem: A clinical study is conducted to assess the role of a vasopressin antagonist in overall survival of patients with advanced heart failure and hyponatremia. After providing informed consent, eligible hospitalized patients are administered either the new drug or a matching placebo along with the appropriate standard care. Assignment to the 2 treatment arms is done randomly using computer-generated numbers. This assignment strategy is most helpful for controlling which of the following?

options.A: Confounding
options.B: Effect modification
options.C: Post-hoc analysis
options.D: Recall bias
options.E: Selective survival

explanations.B: Effect modification results when an external variable positively or negatively impacts the effect of a risk factor on the disease of interest. For instance, the risk of venous thrombosis is increased with estrogen therapy, and this effect is augmented by smoking.
explanations.C: Post-hoc analysis refers to performing unplanned statistical tests on patterns that were identified after the fact in data from a completed study. This can lead to incorrect conclusions, particularly if the appropriate statistical measures have not been taken to account for these additional tests. Post-hoc analysis can be problematic with non-predefined subgroup analysis. Randomization does not directly impact post-hoc analysis (which can be conducted even on data from randomized samples).
explanations.D: Recall bias results from inaccurate recall of past exposure and applies primarily to retrospective studies. People who have suffered an adverse event are more likely to recall risk factors than people without such experiences.
explanations.E: Selective survival bias occurs in case-control studies when cases are selected from the entire disease population instead of just those that are newly diagnosed. For instance, a study on cancer survival that is not limited to newly diagnosed patients will contain a higher proportion of relatively benign malignancies as these patients generally live longer.

generalExplanation:
The effects of confounding bias can be reduced through good study design and proper analysis of the results. Methods used to control for confounding during data analysis include stratified analysis and statistical modeling (eg, multivariate analyses). In addition, methods to control for confounders during study design include the following:
1. Matching: Frequently used in case-control studies, this method involves matching known or suspected confounding variables between the cases and controls. For example, if smoking status is a known confounder, then controls will be selected on a case-by-case basis so that there are similar numbers of smokers and nonsmokers in both the case and control groups.
2. Restriction: This method involves limiting study participation to individuals with specific characteristics. For example, if sex is thought to be a confounder, then a restricted study may enroll only men. However, this method is limited as the study results may not be applicable to the excluded population (ie, women).
3. Randomization: Commonly employed in clinical trials, this technique helps to balance the distribution of confounding variables between treatment and placebo groups so that the unconfounded effect of the exposure of interest can be isolated. An important advantage of randomization, compared to other methods, is the possibility of controlling known risk factors (eg, age and severity of heart failure) as well as the unknown and difficult-to-measure confounders (eg, level of stress and socioeconomic status).

Randomization also eliminates partiality in treatment assignments, minimizing selection bias.
educationalObjective: Randomization is used to control for confounders during the design stage of a study. It helps to control for known, unknown, and difficult-to-measure confounders.

stem: A randomized, controlled 6-month intervention study is conducted using individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or dementia. The objective is to determine if the multicomponent therapy MAKS (a German acronym for motor, activities of daily living, cognitive, social) in day care leads to significantly better progression of activities of daily living and cognitive abilities compared to standard treatment. A total of 362 persons with MCI or dementia took part in the trial, 208 of whom were randomized to the MAKS group and 154 to the control group. At the end of the 6-month intervention phase, the sample consisted of 271 individuals, excluding 55 dropouts in the MAKS group and 36 in the control group. The reasons for dropping out included death, transfer to a different nursing home, termination of day care, and treatment not implemented as indicated. The data analysis is conducted to follow a per-protocol approach. Which of the following describes how the data pertaining to dropouts should be treated to conduct such an analysis?

options.A: Exclude the 36 dropouts in the control group from analysis
options.B: Exclude the 55 dropouts in the MAKS group from analysis
options.C: Exclude the 91 dropouts from analysis
options.D: Keep all 91 dropouts in their respective groups for analysis
options.E: Perform separate analyses for dropouts and nondropouts

explanations.A: In accordance with PP analysis, all 91 dropouts should be excluded from analysis.
explanations.B: In accordance with PP analysis, all 91 dropouts should be excluded from analysis.
explanations.D: An analysis that includes all participants as initially allocated after randomization regardless of what happens during the study period (ie, keeping all 91 dropouts in their respective groups for analysis) follows an intention-to-treat (ITT) principle.
explanations.E: In accordance with PP analysis, all 91 dropouts should be excluded from analysis.

generalExplanation:
Per-protocol (PP) analysis compares treatment groups in a randomized trial by including in the analysis only those participants who strictly adhered (eg, nondropouts) and completed the protocol.

Dropouts may bias estimates of treatment effect. For example, in a placebo-controlled randomized trial of a new drug (ie, treatment vs control group), adverse effects may cause a greater proportion of sicker patients to drop out from the treatment group than from the control group. At the trial's conclusion, the treatment group may end up with a smaller proportion of more severely ill patients than the control group (eg, selection bias). This result could distort the estimation of the effect of a treatment (eg, confounding bias).

By excluding dropouts, PP analysis provides an estimate of the true effect of an intervention assuming a perfect scenario in which all participants were retained and completed treatments as planned. However, this overestimates the effect of the intervention in a realistic (ie, practical) clinical setting, which almost inevitably includes dropouts. In accordance with PP analysis, all 91 dropouts should be excluded from analysis (Choices A, B, and E).

In contrast, an analysis that includes all participants as initially allocated after randomization regardless of what happens during the study period (ie, keeping all 91 dropouts in their respective groups for analysis) follows an intention-to-treat (ITT) principle (Choice D). ITT analysis could lead to a more conservative estimate of the effect of the intervention; however, because it closely mirrors the expected number of dropouts in a real-life situation, ITT analysis reflects the expected effect of the intervention in a realistic (ie, practical) clinical setting.
educationalObjective: Per-protocol analysis includes only those participants who strictly adhered (ie, nondropouts) to the study protocol. This approach tends to provide an estimate of the true effect of an intervention for a perfect scenario, but it overestimates the effect of the intervention in a practical clinical setting.

stem: In an intensive care unit, 10 measurements of a patient's systolic blood pressure were obtained over several hours using an intra-arterial cannula. The maximal value recorded was 120 mm Hg, and the minimal value was 100 mm Hg. If the next measurement shows a value of 240 mm Hg, which of the following is most likely to happen?

options.A: The mean will increase more than the median or the mode
options.B: The median will increase more than the mean or the mode
options.C: The mode will increase more than the mean or the median
options.D: The range will not change
options.E: The standard deviation will not change

explanations.B: The median tends to be more resistant to outliers because it splits an ordered dataset in its middle, where the observations usually do not differ much from one another. For example, the median for the dataset {10, 10, 11, 12, 12} is 11, which splits the dataset in half (comes between {10, 10} and {12, 12}); by adding an additional value of 12, the median will shift to the value between {11, 12}, ie, 11.5. In this case, adding the value of 240 mm Hg will shift the median; however, the change is unlikely to be great, as the first 10 measurements all lie between 100 mm Hg and 120 mm Hg.
explanations.C: The mode (the most frequently observed value) is less likely to be affected by outliers. For example, if the value of 115 mm Hg was recorded most often among the first 10 measurements, then 115 mm Hg would be the mode; having an additional value of 240 mm Hg in the dataset would not change that.
explanations.D: The range is the difference between the maximal value and the minimal value. In this case, the range will change from 20 mm Hg (= 120 − 100 mm Hg) to 140 mm Hg (= 240 − 100 mm Hg).
explanations.E: The standard deviation (a measure of dispersion within the dataset) is sensitive to outliers because outliers significantly increase the dispersion. A value of 240 mm Hg would very likely affect the standard deviation of a dataset of 10 elements, all of which lie between 100 mm Hg and 120 mm Hg.

generalExplanation:
An outlier is defined as an extreme and unusual value observed in a dataset. It may be the result of a recording error, a measurement error, or a natural phenomenon. An outlier can affect the measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode) as well as the measures of dispersion (eg, standard deviation).

The mean (mathematical average) is extremely sensitive to outliers and easily shifts toward them, especially with a small sample size. In this case, the value of 240 mm Hg is an outlier and would cause the mean to increase more than the median or the mode, especially given that there were only 10 total measurements obtained prior to this value, all of which were between 100 and 120 mm Hg.
educationalObjective: An outlier is defined as an extreme and unusual value observed in a dataset. The mean is very sensitive to outliers and easily shifts toward them. The median and mode are more resistant to outliers.

stem:
Objective:
To assess the association of low-dose aspirin use with the performance of two quantitative immunochemical fecal occult blood tests (iFOBTs) in a large sample of patients undergoing colorectal cancer screening

Methods:
Design: Cross-sectional study
Blinding: Technician performing iFOBT tests was blinded to colonoscopy results
Setting: 20 gastroenterology practices in southern Germany
Patients: Patients undergoing screening colonoscopy (mean age 62.1 years) were asked to provide stool samples before the procedure. Information about medication use was collected using a standardized questionnaire. Specific exclusion criteria included the following: visible rectal bleeding or previous positive FOBT result, history of inflammatory bowel disease, colonoscopy in the past 5 years, incomplete colonoscopy, inadequate bowel preparation for colonoscopy, participants with pseudopolyps or histologically undefined polyps at screening colonoscopy, and participants who reported regular use of high-dose analgesics.
Intervention: Two automated, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) based iFOBTs (hemoglobin test and hemoglobin-haptoglobin test) were performed before screening colonoscopy.
Outcome measures: Sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values, and area under receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves in detecting advanced colorectal neoplasms with two quantitative iFOBTs using colonoscopy as gold standard.

Results:
1979 patients (233 regular users of low-dose aspirin and 1746 who never used low-dose aspirin) were studied. Advanced neoplasms were found in 24 users (10.3%) and 181 nonusers (10.4%) of low-dose aspirin.

Conclusion:
For two iFOBTs, low-dose aspirin use affects performance of the test in detecting advanced colorectal neoplasm.
Funding Source: the German Research Foundation, the German Federal Ministry of Education and Research. The test kits were provided free of charge by the manufacturer.
Structured abstract is based on: JAMA. 2010;304(22):2513-20

---

The abstract shown on the left applies to the next 2 items.

A 60-year-old man with known coronary artery disease comes to the physician for a routine check-up. He has no complaints and no abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, or weight loss. His current medications include metoprolol, atorvastatin, and low-dose aspirin. He has no family history of colon cancer. Assuming the study results were statistically significant, which of the following is the best statement concerning the use of iFOBT in this patient?

options.A: Use of low-dose aspirin decreases the accuracy of the test
options.B: Use of low-dose aspirin decreases the sensitivity of the test
options.C: Use of low-dose aspirin increases the sensitivity of the test
options.D: Use of low-dose aspirin increases the specificity of the test

explanations.A: Accuracy can be measured as the total area under the ROC curve. The closer the plotted curve approaches the left and top borders of the graph, the more accurate the test. In this case, the total area under the plotted curve increases with aspirin use (because the increase in sensitivity is larger than the decrease in specificity), leading to an overall increase in test accuracy.
explanations.B: In this study, for a given cut point (eg, 1 µg/g of stool), low-dose aspirin use moves the ROC curve upward; this translates to an increase in sensitivity (eg, from 46% to 70% on the y-axis).
explanations.D: However, aspirin use also causes the curve to shift to the right, indicating a decrease in specificity (eg, from 82% to 79%) as the standard x-axis is (100 - specificity) rather than specificity.

generalExplanation:
The study presented in the abstract assesses the effect of aspirin on the ability of 2 different stool assays to detect colorectal cancer (compared to colonoscopy, the gold standard). The results are given as a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, which is generated by plotting the true-positive rate (sensitivity) against the false-positive rate (1 - specificity). In this study, for a given cut point (eg, 1 µg/g of stool), low-dose aspirin use moves the ROC curve upward; this translates to an increase in sensitivity (eg, from 46% to 70% on the y-axis). However, aspirin use also causes the curve to shift to the right, indicating a decrease in specificity (eg, from 82% to 79%) as the standard x-axis is (100 - specificity) rather than specificity.

Important test parameters given by the ROC curve include the following:
1. Sensitivity: Indicates how well a test can screen for a disease. A higher sensitivity makes it less likely that there are false negatives, meaning that a negative test better rules out the disease (snout).
2. Specificity: Indicates how well a test can confirm the diagnosis. The higher the specificity, the less likely there are false positives, meaning that a positive test result better rules in the condition (spin).
3. Accuracy: Is defined as the proportion of true results (true positive and true negative) out of all the results of a given diagnostic test. Test accuracy depends on the sensitivity and specificity of the test as well as the prevalence of the condition in the population being tested. Accuracy increases as the total area under the ROC curve increases.

Points labeled along the ROC curve represent different quantitative cutoff values for determining positive and negative test results. As the cutoff point is modified, sensitivity and specificity are also changed. With most ROC curves, an increase in sensitivity is offset by a decrease in specificity and vice versa. The ideal diagnostic test is 100% sensitive and specific and provides the most useful information (square line). In contrast, a diagnostic test that provides no useful information demonstrates an inverse linear relationship between sensitivity and specificity (straight line).
educationalObjective: A shift in the receiver operating characteristic curve upward for a given cutoff indicates increased sensitivity. A shift of the curve to the right for a given cutoff point indicates a decrease in specificity.

Item 2 of 2
For patients taking low-dose aspirin, the manufacturer recommends a cutoff point of 1 µg/g for the hemoglobin iFOBT. Changing the test cutoff from 1 µg/g to 4 µg/g would affect the performance of the test in which of the following ways?

options.A: Number of false negatives would decrease
options.B: Number of false positives would decrease
options.C: Number of true positives would increase
options.D: Sensitivity of the test would increase
options.E: Specificity of the test would decrease

explanations.A: By raising the cutoff value, it is harder to obtain a positive test result and easier to obtain a negative result. This will cause the number of false negatives to increase and the number of true positives to decrease, leading to a decrease in sensitivity.
explanations.C: By raising the cutoff value, it is harder to obtain a positive test result and easier to obtain a negative result. This will cause the number of false negatives to increase and the number of true positives to decrease, leading to a decrease in sensitivity.
explanations.D: By raising the cutoff value, it is harder to obtain a positive test result and easier to obtain a negative result. This will cause the number of false negatives to increase and the number of true positives to decrease, leading to a decrease in sensitivity.
explanations.E: The change in cutoff value will also result in an increased number of true negatives and a decreased number of false positives, causing an increase in specificity.

generalExplanation:
Both sensitivity and specificity depend on the cutoff value of a given test. In this example, raising the cutoff value makes it more difficult to detect the condition (colorectal neoplasm) as more hemoglobin must be present in the stool for the test to be positive. By raising the cutoff value, it is harder to obtain a positive test result and easier to obtain a negative result. This will cause the number of false negatives to increase and the number of true positives to decrease, leading to a decrease in sensitivity (Choices A, C, and D). The change in cutoff value will also result in an increased number of true negatives and a decreased number of false positives, causing an increase in specificity (Choice E).

In this case, an increase in the cutoff value from 1 µg/g to 4 µg/g decreases the sensitivity of the hemoglobin test from about 70% to 60% and increases the specificity from about 80% to 90% in patients taking low-dose aspirin. Similarly, the same increase in cutoff values decreases the sensitivity of the hemoglobin-haptoglobin test from about 60% to 40% and increases the specificity from about 80% to 90% in patients taking low-dose aspirin.
educationalObjective: Changing the cutoff value of a test in a way that alters the proportion of true-positive and false-negative results will change the sensitivity. Likewise, a change in the test that modifies the proportion of false-positive and true-negative results will change the specificity.

stem: A study was conducted to assess the relationship between serum HDL2 level (a subfraction of HDL) and carotid intima-media thickness as a marker of atherosclerosis. Interpretation of the results revealed a linear relationship between these 2 variables, with a correlation coefficient r = -0.25 (p = 0.005). Which of the following statements about the results of the study is the most correct?

options.A: As HDL2 level increases, there is an associated decrease in carotid intima-media thickness
options.B: Decreased HDL2 level is the cause of carotid intima-media thickening
options.C: The association is not statistically significant
options.D: There is a strong correlation between HDL2 level and carotid intima-media thickness
options.E: There is a positive correlation between HDL2 level and carotid intima-media thickness

explanations.B: This statement regarding the direction of change does not imply causality.
explanations.C: The association was statistically significant because p <0.05.
explanations.D: The strength of the association was weak because 0.25 is close to 0 (in general r >0.5 or r <-0.5 suggests a strong association, although the exact cutoff depends on what is being studied).
explanations.E: A positive correlation (r >0) would have meant that increases in HDL2 were associated with increases in carotid intima-media thickness.

generalExplanation: The correlation coefficient (r) assesses a linear relationship between 2 variables. The null value for the correlation coefficient is 0 (no association), and the sign of the correlation coefficient indicates a positive or negative association. The closer r is to its margins (-1 or 1), the stronger the association. In this study, as there was a negative correlation between HDL2 and carotid intima-media thickness (given r = -0.25 <0), when there was an increase in one of the variables (eg, HDL2), there was a decrease in the other variable (eg, carotid intima-media thickness). This statement regarding the direction of change does not imply causality (Choice B).
educationalObjective: The correlation coefficient (r) assesses a linear relationship between 2 variables. The null value is 0 (no association), and the sign indicates a positive or negative association.

stem:
A 23-year-old woman comes to the physician at 9 weeks gestation for prenatal counseling. This is her first pregnancy. She has no history of bleeding, and there is no history of hemophilia in her husband's family. However, the patient's father and other relatives have hemophilia A, and she is concerned about the possibility of her child having the disease. The following pedigree is created according to the patient's family history (arrow points to the patient).

Which of the following is the best response to this patient's concern?

options.A: The chance of having hemophilia does not depend on the child's sex
options.B: The probability of having a child who is a silent carrier is 50%
options.C: The probability of having a child with hemophilia is 25%
options.D: The probability of having a child with hemophilia is 50%
options.E: The probability of having a child with hemophilia is similar to that of the general population

explanations.A: Hemophilia is an X-linked recessive disorder and is much more common in males.
explanations.B: On average, 25% of this patient's children would be expected to have hemophilia A, 25% would be silent carriers, and 50% would be unaffected.
explanations.D: On average, 25% of this patient's children would be expected to have hemophilia A, 25% would be silent carriers, and 50% would be unaffected.
explanations.E: The incidence of hemophilia in the general population is <1%, but the probability of this patient having a child with hemophilia is 25%.

generalExplanation:
Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disease caused by a deficit in coagulation factor VIII. All daughters born to a father with hemophilia A and an unaffected mother will be carriers. If the father has hemophilia A and the mother is a carrier, then half of the daughters will likely be carriers and the other half will likely inherit the mutation from both parents and have hemophilia themselves.

This patient is a silent carrier of hemophilia A. Half of her sons will will have hemophilia A, and the probability of having a male child is 50%; therefore, the overall probability of having a son with hemophilia is 25% and an unaffected son is 25% (0.5 x 0.5 = 0.25). As this patient is a carrier, half of her daughters will be asymptomatic carriers. The chance of having a girl is also 50%, which makes the chance of having a silent carrier daughter 25% and an unaffected daughter also 25%.
educationalObjective: Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder. On average, carrier mothers and unaffected fathers have a 25% chance of having a son with hemophilia, a silent carrier daughter, an unaffected son, or an unaffected daughter.

A study is conducted to evaluate the amino acid phenylalanine in preterm newborns who were fed different human milk diets. Twenty-four very low-weight preterm newborns are randomly assigned to one of the following feeding groups:
• Group I: banked human milk plus 5% commercial fortifier with bovine protein
• Group II: banked human milk plus evaporated fortifier derived from modified human milk
• Group III: banked human milk plus lyophilized fortifier derived from modified human milk

The newborns receive the group diet until full diet is attained at 15 days. Plasma amino acid analysis is performed on the first and last day of feeding. Analysis of data includes an analysis of variance (ANOVA) to compare group mean levels of phenylalanine in plasma at Day 0 and at Day 15, along with 95% confidence intervals to estimate ANOVA-adjusted means for each group at each time point. An excerpt of results is shown below:

Based on these findings, which of the following statements is justified?

options.A: Group II shows a significant decrease in mean plasma phenylalanine levels from Day 0 to Day 15.
options.B: Results suggest a statistically significant difference in mean plasma phenylalanine levels between all 3 groups at Day 15.
options.C: The only group to show evidence of a significant increase in mean plasma phenylalanine levels from Day 0 to Day 15 is Group III.
options.D: There is evidence of a significant increase in mean plasma phenylalanine levels in all 3 groups from Day 0 to Day 15.
options.E: There is no statistically significant difference in mean plasma phenylalanine levels between any specific groups at either Day 0 or Day 15.

explanations.A: In addition, the CIs at Day 0 and Day 15 for Groups I and II overlap. This indicates that in Groups I and II, there may or may not be a significant difference in means from Day 0 to Day 15.
explanations.B: The CIs for Groups I and II at Day 15 overlap, so there may or may not be a significant difference in means between these 2 groups at Day 15.
explanations.D: In addition, the CIs at Day 0 and Day 15 for Groups I and II overlap. This indicates that in Groups I and II, there may or may not be a significant difference in means from Day 0 to Day 15.
explanations.E: The ANOVA test at Day 0 shows no evidence of a significant difference between group means (p = 0.93); however, the ANOVA test at Day 15 shows that at least 1 group mean is different from the rest (p = 0.01).

generalExplanation:
Analysis of variance (ANOVA) compares the means of ≥3 independent groups. However, a statistically significant ANOVA (ie, p-value is below the significance level, usually 0.05) indicates only that at least 1 group mean is different from the rest. Therefore, further evaluation is required to determine which group means differ. It is possible to use confidence intervals (CIs) to determine whether means of >2 groups are different.
• If CIs do not overlap, there is a significant difference between the groups' means.
• If CIs overlap, there may or may not be a significant difference between the groups' means.

In this question, ANOVA is used to determine whether the mean levels of phenylalanine in plasma differ between 3 feeding groups. The ANOVA test at Day 0 shows no evidence of a significant difference between group means (p = 0.93); however, the ANOVA test at Day 15 shows that at least 1 group mean is different from the rest (p = 0.01) (Choice E).

The CIs for Groups I and II at Day 15 overlap, so there may or may not be a significant difference in means between these 2 groups at Day 15 (Choice B). However, the CI for Group III at Day 15 does not overlap with the CI for either Group I or II at Day 15, so the mean in Group III at Day 15 is significantly different from that of Groups I and II at Day 15.

In addition, the CIs at Day 0 and Day 15 for Groups I and II overlap. This indicates that in Groups I and II, there may or may not be a significant difference in means from Day 0 to Day 15 (Choices A and D). By contrast, the CIs at Day 0 and Day 15 for Group III do not overlap, so in Group III there is a significant difference in means from Day 0 to Day 15, with the mean at Day 15 being higher (ie, increase in mean).

Therefore, the only group to show evidence of a significant increase in mean plasma phenylalanine levels from Day 0 to Day 15 is Group III.
educationalObjective: Analysis of variance (ANOVA) compares the means of independent groups and determines only whether at least 2 group means differ. Nonoverlapping confidence intervals always imply a statistically significant difference between groups; however, the opposite is not necessarily true.

stem: An 80-year-old woman with multiple medical problems is admitted to the hospital for evaluation of syncope. Her heart rate is found to be 36/min. She was admitted to another hospital recently, then discharged to an acute rehabilitation facility, and then sent to a nursing home. Review of her history shows that the patient is taking high-dose diltiazem, metoprolol, and atenolol. Which of the following medication reconciliation interventions is most likely to result in a decrease in adverse drug events and health care utilization?

options.A: Educational booklets distributed to patients
options.B: Educational booklets distributed to physicians
options.C: Information technology-related interventions
options.D: Nurse and nurse assistant-directed interventions
options.E: Pharmacist-directed interventions

explanations.A: Objective studies to identify best practices for medication reconciliation have been limited, with few interventions confirmed to improve quality of care.
explanations.B: Objective studies to identify best practices for medication reconciliation have been limited, with few interventions confirmed to improve quality of care.
explanations.C: Objective studies to identify best practices for medication reconciliation have been limited, with few interventions confirmed to improve quality of care.
explanations.D: Objective studies to identify best practices for medication reconciliation have been limited, with few interventions confirmed to improve quality of care.

generalExplanation:
Transitions of care - between inpatient and outpatient facilities and between units within inpatient facilities - are potential sources of medical error. In particular, continuity of care for medications is especially problematic, and errors can lead to an increased risk of medical complications as well as cost. As a result, most inpatient facilities in the United States have instituted protocols to improve the accuracy of the medication record during transitions of care.

Objective studies to identify best practices for medication reconciliation have been limited, with few interventions confirmed to improve quality of care (Choices A, B, C, and D). However, interventions that target pharmacy personnel and high-risk patients in particular appear to have the most impact on the quality of patient care.
educationalObjective: Continuity of care for medications at the time of transitions of care, between inpatient and outpatient facilities and within inpatient facilities, is a potential source of medical error. Interventions that target pharmacy personnel and high-risk patients appear to be the most effective in improving the quality of patient care.

A 67-year-old man recently diagnosed with coronary artery disease comes to the physician for a follow-up appointment. He was hospitalized for congestive heart failure 4 weeks ago and underwent coronary angiography showing significant narrowing of left anterior descending and right coronary arteries with <50% stenosis. The patient's left ventricular ejection fraction is 30%. Prior to starting medication, he could walk only 3 blocks on a flat surface before experiencing chest discomfort and shortness of breath. However, now he is symptomatic only with strenuous physical activity. During the appointment, the patient asks about the risks and benefits of coronary bypass surgery. Based on the study results, which of the following is the best statement?

options.A: Surgery carries a higher short-term risk of dying
options.B: Surgery causes increased risk of heart failure exacerbation
options.C: Surgery leads to more procedures over the long term
options.D: Surgery would not affect overall long-term quality of life
options.E: The benefits of surgery are limited to preventing a heart attack

explanations.B: The hazard ratio for death due to any cause or hospitalization for heart failure was 0.84 (CI=[0.71-0.98], p=0.03). This means that surgery in addition to medical therapy improves heart failure symptoms compared to medical therapy alone as all-cause mortality was not significantly different between the 2 groups (given p = 0.12 as explained above).
explanations.C: The hazard ratio for death due to any cause or revascularization was 0.60 (CI=[0.51-0.71], p <0.001). This indicates that the surgery in addition to medical therapy leads to fewer revascularization procedures than medical therapy alone, since all-cause mortality is not significantly different between the 2 groups.
explanations.D: The hazard ratio for death or hospitalization due to any cause was 0.81 (CI=[0.71-0.93], p=0.003). This indicates that the surgery added to medical therapy leads to fewer hospitalizations than medical therapy alone because all-cause mortality was not significantly different between the 2 groups. Fewer hospitalizations help to improve patient quality of life.
explanations.E: All the secondary outcomes except 30-day mortality were favorable for surgery with medical therapy, indicating that there are other benefits to surgery with medical therapy aside from heart attack prevention.

generalExplanation:
The study presented in the abstract is a randomized clinical trial comparing the benefit of coronary-artery bypass grafting (CABG) with medical therapy versus medical therapy alone for the management of coronary artery disease and heart failure (defined as <35% left ventricular ejection fraction [EF]). This patient meets the inclusion criteria for the study (EF <35%, coronary artery disease with <50% stenosis [patients with >50% stenosis were excluded from the study], minimal symptoms while receiving medical therapy), so the study findings are likely to apply to him.

The results of the study are reported in terms of the hazard ratio, which is the ratio of an event rate occurring in the treatment group compared to an event rate occurring in the non-treatment group. A ratio <1 indicates that the treatment group had a lower event rate and a value >1 indicates that the treatment group had a higher event rate.

In this study, overall mortality was the primary end point. The hazard ratio for all-cause mortality was 0.86 (CI=[0.72-1.04], p=0.12). However, the p-value is >0.05, meaning that there was no significant difference in all-cause mortality between the study groups during the average follow-up period of 56 months. In contrast, CABG with medical therapy was associated with a significantly higher mortality in the first 30 days after randomization than medical therapy alone, with a hazard ratio of 3.12 (CI=[1.33-7.31], p=0.006). This is most likely due to the inherent risks of surgery and related short-term postoperative complications (risks that should be explicitly conveyed to the patient).
educationalObjective: Hazard ratios are the ratio of an event rate occurring in the treatment group versus the non-treatment group. Ratios <1 indicate that the treatment group had a lower event rate and ratios >1 indicate that the treatment group had a higher event rate.

Item 2 of 2
At the end of the follow-up period, investigators reported that 17% of patients in the medical therapy group and 91% of patients in the medical therapy plus CABG group underwent CABG. Combining both groups and then analyzing outcomes for patients who actually underwent CABG versus those who received only medical therapy might introduce which of the following?

options.A: Lead-time bias
options.B: Measurement bias
options.C: Observer bias
options.D: Recall bias
options.E: Selection bias

explanations.A: Lead-time bias happens when two disease interventions are compared and one diagnoses the disease earlier than the other without an effect on the outcome (eg, survival). This would make it appear that the intervention prolonged survival when it really just diagnosed the disease sooner.
explanations.B: Measurement bias occurs from poor data collection with inaccurate results (not described in this case).
explanations.C: Observer bias occurs when the observer is influenced by prior knowledge or details of the study in a way that affects the results. Studies attempt to avoid this bias by blinding observers from knowing treatment assignments and by measuring objective outcomes (eg, mortality) that are less likely to be skewed by observers. Observer bias could potentially be present from the outset as this study was not blinded. However, changing the type of data analysis would not introduce this bias.
explanations.D: Recall bias occurs when a study participant's answer to a question is affected by prior exposures. However, this is more common in retrospective studies rather than prospective studies such as randomized clinical trials.

generalExplanation:
The study presented in the abstract is a randomized clinical trial comparing the benefit of CABG with medical therapy versus medical therapy alone. Despite high-quality medical therapy provided to all patients in the study, 17% of patients in the medical therapy group clinically deteriorated to the point where CABG was uncontrovertibly indicated. When the treatment regimen selected for a patient depends on the severity of the patient's condition, a form of selection bias known as susceptibility bias (confounding by indication) can result. This occurs because surgery patients arising from the medical therapy group may have underlying confounders that were responsible for worsening of their disease. Grouping them with patients from the surgery group may lead to erroneous analysis and weaken the conclusions that can be drawn from the study.

To avoid selection bias in studies, patients are randomly assigned to treatments to minimize potential confounding variables. Many studies also perform an intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis to deal with selection bias. An ITT analysis compares the initial randomized treatment groups (the original intention) regardless of the eventual treatment to avoid counting crossover patients. Conversely, as-treated analysis (suggested in question stem) compares the groups based on the actual treatment received. An as-treated analysis is performed to gauge the effectiveness of the treatment itself, with less regard for potential confounders.
educationalObjective: When the treatment regimen selected for a patient depends on the severity of the patient's condition, a form of selection bias known as susceptibility bias (confounding by indication) can result. To avoid selection bias in studies, patients are randomly assigned to treatments to minimize potential confounding variables. Many studies also perform an intention-to-treat analysis, which compares the initial randomized treatment groups (the original intention) regardless of the eventual treatment.

Objective
To compare the effects of a brown rice–based vegan diet to a standard diabetic diet on glycemic control.

Methods
Design: Open, randomized controlled trial without participant blinding.
Follow-up period: 0, 12 weeks.
Participants: 118 patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Inclusion criteria: age 30-70; taking oral antidiabetic agents for ≥6 months; hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) level of 6%-10%. Exclusion criteria: increase in dose of antidiabetic agent or addition of new antidiabetic agent in past 3 months.
Intervention: Vegan diet (n = 59) versus standard diabetic diet (n = 59) for 12 weeks. Compliance reported based on a self-assessment daily dietary record allowing standardized conversion to a percentage scale.
Outcomes: Primary endpoints: change in HbA1c level over 12 weeks. Secondary endpoints include change in BMI and in waist circumference.

Results
An excerpt of results for Week 0, Week 12, and Change (Week 12 – Week 0) is shown below.
*Values represent means ± standard deviations. The p-values for tests comparing the mean change in primary endpoint between the 2 diet groups were statistically significant regardless of compliance.
**p < 0.01; p-values for paired t-test to determine whether changes from Week 0 to Week 12 are significantly different from 0.

---

The abstract shown on the left applies to the next 2 items.

A 46-year-old woman comes to the office for follow-up of type 2 diabetes mellitus. The patient has been following a standard diabetic diet and the same oral antidiabetic agent regimen for the past 8 months. BMI is 25.2 kg/m², waist circumference is 83 cm, and hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) is 7.3%. The patient recently read an article comparing a vegan diet to a standard diabetic diet in control of HbA1c levels. An excerpt from the study abstract is shown.

Item 1 of 2
Based on the abstract, which of the following conclusions is most appropriate?

options.A: Baseline difference in waist circumference between the participants in the vegan and the standard diabetic diet groups makes comparisons unreliable
options.B: Compared to participants in the standard diabetic diet group, participants in the vegan diet group had a greater, statistically significant reduction in BMI
options.C: None of the differences between Week 0 and Week 12 reported in the abstract demonstrates any clinical significance
options.D: Only participants with ≥90% compliance who followed a vegan diet showed a statistically significant decrease in HbA1c level at 12 weeks

explanations.A: Although the baseline waist circumference values were 84.0 ± 9.8 in the vegan group and 82.3 ± 7.5 in the standard group, these differences likely are not statistically significant given how close these means are to each other and the magnitude of the standard deviation in each group (ie, vegan group 9.8 vs standard group 7.5).
explanations.C: The vegan diet produced clinically significant reductions in HbA1c (eg, −0.5, −0.9), similar to those that can be achieved with pharmacotherapy.
explanations.D: HbA1c levels were significantly reduced in both the vegan and the standard groups (p < 0.01 for change in HbA1c in both groups), with a greater reduction in the vegan group (−0.5 ± 0.8) compared to the standard group (−0.2 ± 0.7). Among participants with ≥90% compliance, the reductions in HbA1c levels were even larger (−0.9 in the vegan group, −0.3 in the standard group). The p-values comparing the reductions between the 2 diet groups were statistically significant, regardless of compliance.

generalExplanation:
This study compared the effects of a vegan diet to a standard diabetic diet on glycemic control in select patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. The endpoints of the study were change in hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) level over 12 weeks (primary endpoint) and changes in BMI, waist circumference, and other variables (secondary endpoints). Negative values for the changes (eg, −0.5) represent reductions; the standard deviations (eg, ±0.8) describe the spread of the changes (even though some values cross 0, they do not help determine statistical significance because they reflect spread, not confidence intervals). According to the table, p-values < 0.01 for paired t-tests were considered statistically significant.

Based on the abstract:
• HbA1c levels were significantly reduced in both the vegan and the standard groups (p < 0.01 for change in HbA1c in both groups), with a greater reduction in the vegan group (−0.5 ± 0.8) compared to the standard group (−0.2 ± 0.7). Among participants with ≥90% compliance, the reductions in HbA1c levels were even larger (−0.9 in the vegan group, −0.3 in the standard group) (Choice D). The p-values comparing the reductions between the 2 diet groups were statistically significant, regardless of compliance.
• BMI was significantly reduced (p < 0.01) in the vegan group only. Compared to the standard group (−0.1 ± 0.6), the vegan group had a greater reduction in BMI (−0.5 ± 0.9) at 12 weeks.
• Waist circumference was significantly reduced (p < 0.01) in the vegan group only. Compared to the standard group (−0.8 ± 4.6), the vegan group had a greater reduction in waist circumference (−3.1 ± 4.9).

Although both diets led to reductions in HbA1c levels, only the vegan diet helped to significantly reduce BMI and waist circumference.
educationalObjective: Statistically significant changes are reflected by a p-value less than a given significance level (eg, p < 0.01).

Which of the following recommendations is appropriate for this patient?

options.A: A vegan diet cannot be recommended because the study's limited follow-up period means that the results are not reproducible
options.B: A vegan diet cannot be recommended because the study's participants were not adequately blinded to the assigned diet
options.C: Although a vegan diet helped with weight loss in this study, the results may not apply to the patient given her BMI
options.D: Although a vegan diet may be more helpful than a standard diabetic diet in decreasing HbA1c level, the patient may find compliance difficult

explanations.A: The adequate follow-up time in a study depends on various factors, including the time required to observe a sufficiently large effect (eg, change in HbA1c level) in a study group to make valid statistical inferences (eg, 12-week follow-up chosen because HbA1c measures 3-month blood glucose averages). Although a longer follow-up period may potentially clarify effect duration and identify longterm side effects, study reproducibility (ie, in similar conditions) is not likely to be affected by a limited follow-up period.
explanations.B: Although blinding is commonly used in experimental studies to control for bias, there are some instances in which blinding participants is impossible, as in interventions consisting of diet regimens or surgery.
explanations.C: Although BMI was not a criterion used to include or exclude participants in the study, having a BMI close to the study's baseline values helps make a better application of study results. The patient's BMI (25.2 kg/m²) is within the range of the baseline BMI values in the study (eg, 23.9 ± 3.4); therefore, it does not suggest that the study results would not apply.

The applicability of study results beyond the specific population studied depends on whether particular patients are similar to those studied. This patient is a 46-year-old woman who has type 2 diabetes mellitus, a BMI of 25.2 kg/m², and an HbA1c level of 7.3%; she has been following a standard diabetic diet and antidiabetic agent regimen for the past 8 months. Based on the inclusion (ie, age 30-70; taking oral antidiabetic agents for ≥6 months; HbA1c level of 6%-10%) and exclusion (ie, increase in dose of antidiabetic agent or addition of new antidiabetic agent in past 3 months; current vegetarian; chronic renal failure) criteria described in the abstract, the study results may apply to her.

The study demonstrated that a vegan diet may be more helpful than a standard diabetic diet in decreasing HbA1c level, particularly among patients with a high (≥90%) compliance. However, only 15 of 59 (~25%) of participants achieved ≥90% compliance in the vegan group. Therefore, although a vegan diet likely would be beneficial to reduce this patient's HbA1c level, compliance may be difficult.
educationalObjective: The applicability of study results beyond the specific population studied depends on whether particular patients are similar to those studied. Compliance to treatments can be an important factor.

stem: In a large population with an almost negligible growth rate and minimal migration, the incidence of type 2 diabetes mellitus is 3 cases per 1,000 individuals a year, and has been stable for the last 30 years. However, the prevalence of type 2 diabetes mellitus has increased progressively over the same period. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this trend over time?

options.A: Decreased length of hospital stay
options.B: High mortality in patients with diabetes
options.C: Improved disease management
options.D: Increased diagnostic accuracy
options.E: Selective survival bias

explanations.A: Decreased length of hospital stay is not helpful in explaining the increased prevalence described in this case.
explanations.B: A high mortality rate in patients diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus would result in a decrease, rather than an increase, in prevalence.
explanations.D: Increased diagnostic accuracy would significantly increase both incidence and prevalence of disease.
explanations.E: Selective survival bias refers to the selection process of prevalent cases rather than incident cases in a case-control study.

generalExplanation:
Incidence and prevalence are 2 important concepts in epidemiology that measure disease occurrence in a population:
• Incidence (incident cases) refers to the number of new cases of disease that develop in a specific population over a specified time period.
• By contrast, prevalence quantifies existing cases of disease in the population at a particular point in time.

Prevalence of disease depends on how fast cases develop and on the duration of the disease. When a population has reached a stable condition, as suggested by a negligible growth rate (ie, neither growing nor shrinking in size) and minimal migration, the prevalence of disease can be approximated by considering the incidence and the duration of disease in the following manner:
Prevalence = (Incidence) × (Duration of disease)

In this case, the specific population has a rising prevalence but a stable incidence of diabetes. In other words, more people are being documented as having diabetes although the number of people being newly diagnosed each year remains the same. Because incidence is stable, the increasing prevalence can likely be attributed to factors that prolong the duration of the disease, such as improvements in quality of care and disease management, which may lead to a significant increase in life expectancy.
educationalObjective: An increasing prevalence but stable incidence of a disease can be attributed to factors that prolong the duration of the disease (eg, improved quality of care and disease management).

stem: A group of investigators is studying the relationship between a particular 5-lipoxygenase genotype and atherosclerosis. A random sample of patients from a local university hospital is invited to participate in the study. Blood samples for leukocyte genotyping are obtained, and ultrasonography to assess carotid intima-media thickness (CIMT), a marker of atherosclerosis, is performed. Results show that the particular 5-lipoxygenase genotype is associated with abnormally increased CIMT, a predisposition to atherosclerosis. Which of the following best describes this study design?

options.A: Case-control study
options.B: Cross-sectional study
options.C: Prospective cohort study
options.D: Randomized clinical trial
options.E: Retrospective cohort study

explanations.A: A case-control study is designed by selecting both patients with a particular disease (cases) and patients without that disease (controls), and then determining their previous exposure status. In this case, the researchers selected a single sample from the target population and categorized subjects according to their presence or absence of the risk factor (ie, a particular 5-lipoxygenase genotype) and disease (ie, CIMT status) at a single point in time.
explanations.C: In cohort studies, a group of exposed and unexposed subjects is followed over time for development of the outcome of interest. Contrary to the prospective cohort study, in the retrospective case, exposure and outcome have already occurred at the beginning of the study; therefore, exposure and outcome status are ascertained retrospectively. In both prospective and retrospective cohort studies, however, there is a follow-up of exposed and unexposed individuals across time. By contrast, in this example, a snapshot of the subjects was obtained at one particular time.
explanations.D: A randomized clinical trial is an experimental study that directly compares ≥2 treatments or interventions. Typically, the subjects are randomly assigned to an intervention (eg, a medication) or placebo, and then followed for the development of the outcome of interest (eg, disease).
explanations.E: In cohort studies, a group of exposed and unexposed subjects is followed over time for development of the outcome of interest. Contrary to the prospective cohort study, in the retrospective case, exposure and outcome have already occurred at the beginning of the study; therefore, exposure and outcome status are ascertained retrospectively. In both prospective and retrospective cohort studies, however, there is a follow-up of exposed and unexposed individuals across time. By contrast, in this example, a snapshot of the subjects was obtained at one particular time.

generalExplanation:
A cross-sectional study is an observational study design that may be employed to estimate the prevalence of disease, or to examine associations between risk factors and disease as they exist in a well-defined population at one particular time. This type of design typically takes a snapshot and measures prevalence of risk factor and outcome simultaneously.

In this case, subjects are classified according to their risk factor (ie, presence or absence of the particular 5-lipoxygenase genotype) and disease status (ie, presence or absence of abnormally increased carotid intima-media thickness [CIMT]) at the same time (ie, snapshot). Then, the association between the presence of the risk factor and the disease is estimated. A major limitation of cross-sectional studies is that the temporal relationship between risk factor and disease is not always clear. In this example, however, demonstrating a temporal relationship is possible due to the nature of the risk factor (acquiring a particular genotype precedes atherosclerosis).
educationalObjective: In a cross-sectional study, risk factor and outcome are measured simultaneously at a particular point in time (snapshot study). In other study designs, a certain period separates the exposure from the outcome.

stem: A randomized placebo-controlled trial is conducted to compare the effectiveness of a new drug versus placebo for the treatment of hallucinations and delusions associated with Parkinson disease (PD). A total of 60 patients diagnosed with severe PD psychosis are randomly assigned to receive either the new drug (n = 30) or placebo (n = 30). The primary outcome is change in PD-Adapted Scale for Assessment of Positive Symptoms (SAPS-PD). A group of independent and blinded raters administered the SAPS-PD to measure the frequency and severity of hallucinations and delusions of all participants at baseline and week 6. The results of the study showed that the new drug is significantly more effective in reducing the frequency and severity of hallucinations and delusions (p < 0.01). Compared to an unblinded trial, which of the following is the effect of including a group of independent, blinded raters in this trial?

options.A: Decreases loss to follow-up
options.B: Decreases nonresponse bias
options.C: Decreases statistical power
options.D: Increases external validity
options.E: Increases internal validity

explanations.A: An unequal loss of participants from study groups in follow-up (eg, cohort, experimental) studies is known as attrition bias. This study provides no information to evaluate attrition.
explanations.B: Nonresponse bias may occur when a proportion of study participants become nonrespondents. Nonresponse typically affects studies that use questionnaires or surveys to collect data from participants. This study provides no information to evaluate nonresponse bias.
explanations.C: Failure to show a statistically significant association between a treatment and an outcome is often due to insufficient power (eg, due to a small sample size) to detect an association. This study showed a significant difference between groups (p < 0.01), so the study had sufficient power to provide evidence of a causal relationship.
explanations.D: Because the study enrolled only patients with severe PD-related psychosis, its results only generalize to this specific population of patients. This choice of study population reduces the study's external validity (the applicability of study results beyond the specific population studied).

generalExplanation:
Internal validity refers to the ability of a study design to provide evidence of a causal relationship between a treatment (eg, new drug) and an outcome (eg, hallucinations). The internal validity of a study is threatened when factors other than the treatment can potentially explain the relationship found in a study. One such factor is measurement bias—the misclassification of exposure and/or outcome (eg, labeling diseased as nondiseased and vice versa) in a study. Blinding those who collect or measure data in a study reduces the likelihood of measurement bias that arises from being aware of treatment assignments and, consequently, increases the internal validity of the study.

In this trial, participants diagnosed with severe Parkinson disease (PD) psychosis are randomly assigned to receive either the new drug or placebo. The study employed a group of independent and blinded raters to administer the PD-Adapted Scale for Assessment of Positive Symptoms and measure the frequency and severity of symptoms for all participants. Blinding those who collect and measure data to the treatment each participant is receiving reduces measurement bias, which ultimately increases the internal validity of the study.
educationalObjective: Internal validity refers to the ability of a research design to provide evidence of a causal relationship between a treatment and an outcome. Blinding increases the internal validity of a study.

stem: A study compares the efficacy of postpartum oral cephalexin in combination with metronidazole versus placebo to decrease surgical site infection rates among women with obesity who have already received standard preoperative antimicrobial prophylaxis and undergone cesarean delivery. The absolute risk reduction between the cephalexin-metronidazole group and the placebo group is 10.0%. In the placebo group, the surgical site infection rate is 16.0%. In the cephalexin-metronidazole group, there are 12 patients with surgical site infection. Based on this information, which of the following is the approximate number of patients in the cephalexin-metronidazole group?
generalExplanation:
Absolute risk reduction (ARR) describes the difference in the rate (or risk) of an unfavorable outcome between the treatment group (eg, new treatment) and the control group (eg, standard treatment):
ARR = (Risk_control − Risk_treatment)

In this study, Risk_control is the rate of surgical site infections in the group treated with placebo and Risk_treatment is the rate of surgical site infections in the group treated with cephalexin-metronidazole. It is given that ARR = 0.10 (ie, 10%) and Rate_control is 0.16 (ie, 16%); therefore, the value of Rate_treatment is:
ARR = Rate_control − Rate_treatment
0.10 = 0.16 − Rate_treatment
Rate_treatment = 0.16 − 0.10 = 0.06

Rate_treatment is equal to the number of surgical site infections in the cephalexin-metronidazole group divided by the number of patients in that group (ie, sample size, n). Therefore, it is possible to use the calculated Rate_treatment (ie, 0.06) and the given number of surgical site infections in the cephalexin-metronidazole group (ie, 12) to determine the sample size n of that group as follows:
Rate_treatment = (number of infections) / n
0.06 = 12 / n
n = 200

The number of patients in the cephalexin-metronidazole group is 200.
educationalObjective: Absolute risk reduction (ARR) = Risk_control − Risk_treatment.

stem: A clinical trial is performed to study the effect of a new antihypertensive drug. If the subjects of the study change their behavior because they are aware that they are under observation, what type of bias will take place?

options.A: Sample distortion bias
options.B: Information bias
options.C: Confounding bias
options.D: Hawthorne effect
options.E: Not a source of bias

explanations.A: Sample distortion bias is seen when the estimate of exposure and outcome association is biased because the study sample is not representative of the target population with respect to the joint distribution of exposure and outcome.
explanations.B: Information bias occurs due to the imperfect assessment of association between the exposure and outcome as a result of errors in the measurement of exposure and outcome status. It can be minimized by using standardized techniques for surveillance and measurement of outcomes, as well as trained observers to measure the exposure and outcome.
explanations.C: Confounding bias occurs due to the presence of one or more variables associated independently with both the exposure and the outcome. For example, cigarette smoking can be a confounding factor in studying the association between maternal alcohol drinking and low birth weight babies, as cigarette smoking is independently associated with both alcohol consumption and low birth weight babies.

generalExplanation:
Bias poses a threat to the validity of any study. A sample which is not representative of the population is said to be a biased sample. In this vignette, a biased sample with Hawthorne effect is described.

Hawthorne effect can be defined as the tendency of a study population to affect the outcome because these people are aware that they are being studied. This awareness leads to a consequent change in behavior while under observation, thereby seriously affecting the validity of the study. Hawthorne effect is commonly seen in studies that concern behavioral outcomes or outcomes that can be influenced by behavioral changes. In order to minimize the potential of the Hawthorne effect, studied subjects can be kept unaware that they are being studied; however, this may pose ethical problems. Randomized control trials have a sense of uncertainty and risk due to randomization, which may be more potent behavior modifiers than mere observation.
educationalObjective: Hawthorne effect is the tendency of a study population to affect the outcome because they are aware that they are being studied.

stem: A recent study evaluated the efficacy of a new quadrivalent vaccine in preventing the development of human papilloma virus (HPV) infection–related external genital lesions in boys and men age 16 to 26. A total of 1,320 healthy boys and men who were initially negative for all four vaccine HPV types were given the new vaccine and followed for 3 years. At the end of the follow-up, 24 participants had developed external genital lesions. Which of the following is the most likely reason no conclusion regarding vaccine efficacy can be drawn from these results?

options.A: The follow-up period of 3 years is too short
options.B: The number who developed external genital lesions is too small
options.C: The sample consisted of only boys and men age 16 to 26
options.D: The trial did not assess genital lesion development in unvaccinated boys and men age 16 to 26
options.E: The vaccine efficacy in preventing genital lesions is close to 98%

explanations.A: Most genital lesions appear within a few months of HPV infection; therefore, a 3-year follow-up offers sufficient time for the development and diagnosis of external genital lesions.
explanations.B: The small number of individuals who developed external genital lesions compared to the total may alter some aspect of the statistical analysis (eg, increase error, lower statistical power). However, the reason no conclusion about VE can be drawn from these results is the absence of a control group of unvaccinated individuals.
explanations.C: Boys and men age 16 to 26 are the study's population of interest; therefore, all conclusions generalize to this population (although they may not generalize to other populations).
explanations.E: However, the study does not include an unvaccinated group (ie, control group); therefore, it is not possible to draw conclusions about VE.

generalExplanation:
This study is concerned with the efficacy of a new quadrivalent vaccine to prevent the development of human papilloma virus (HPV) infection–related external genital lesions in boys and men age 16 to 26. Vaccine efficacy (VE) is calculated by estimating the risk of disease in a group of vaccinated individuals and in a group of unvaccinated individuals and then determining the percentage reduction among vaccinated individuals relative to unvaccinated individuals.

VE = (risk of disease in unvaccinated − risk of disease in vaccinated) / (risk of disease in unvaccinated)

The greater the percentage reduction of illness in the vaccinated group, the greater the VE.

A total of 1,320 healthy boys and men age 16 to 26 were enrolled in the study and given the new vaccine. The study results showed that 24 of 1,320 vaccinated individuals developed external genital lesions; therefore, the risk of development of external genital lesions among vaccinated individuals is 24/1,320 = 0.0182, or 1.82%. This means that about 100% − 1.82% = 98.18% of vaccinated individuals did not develop external genital lesions.

However, the study does not include an unvaccinated group (ie, control group); therefore, it is not possible to draw conclusions about VE (Choice E). For example, unvaccinated individuals may have developed lesions at the same rate of ~1.82%, suggesting the vaccine had no efficacy.
educationalObjective: Vaccine efficacy is calculated by estimating the risk of disease in a group of vaccinated individuals and in a group of unvaccinated individuals (ie, control group) and then determining the percentage reduction among vaccinated individuals relative to unvaccinated individuals.
